app.title: MARS OS
app.aboutText: MARS OS layers real NASA and USGS data on an editable 3D Mars. Original data is never modified: every terrain change is a proposal with evidence, confidence and an approval status, stored in a revertible version history. Simulated content is always labelled.

how.title: How the history works
how.one: The terrain starts from NASA elevation data (version 1).
how.two: A person or Gemini proposes a local change, with evidence and sources (AI tab).
how.three: Only when a person approves it does the change become a new version here, with its author and reason.
how.four: You can compare versions, view the map as it was, and restore any earlier version: nothing is ever deleted.
how.empty: There are no approved changes on this map yet, so the history has only the original version. To see how it works with example edits, open the demo sandbox (separate storage):

routes.intro: Compare two walking routes between A and B on the current terrain: the shortest one and the one with gentlest slopes. Values come from the elevation data; limits are your planning assumptions.
routes.assumptionsNote: Editable assumptions for this prototype, not validated EVA rules.

rec.lowSlope: Take the low-slope route: it is only {{extra}}% longer and its steepest section is {{slope}}° gentler ({{lowMax}}° vs {{shortMax}}°).
rec.tradeoff: Trade-off: the low-slope route is {{extra}}% longer but {{slope}}° gentler at its steepest point ({{lowMax}}° vs {{shortMax}}°). Choose by suit, load and time budget.
rec.similar: Both routes are similar in steepness (max {{shortMax}}° vs {{lowMax}}°): the shortest route is the reasonable choice.
rec.lowSlopeSame: Take the low-slope route: practically the same length, and its steepest section is {{slope}}° gentler ({{lowMax}}° vs {{shortMax}}°).

routes.recBasis: Computed from measured elevation on a {{cell}} m grid, by fixed rules (no AI).
routes.dataWarn: Part of a route crosses terrain where only coarse elevation data exists: slopes there are smoothed and may be underestimated.
routes.rocks: Routes are computed on a {{cell}} m grid from the best elevation available; zoom in with the HiRISE 25 cm layer to see metre-scale rocks along the way.
routes.changeAdded: New terrain edits in the area
routes.changePreview: A pending proposal preview is shown — not an approved change.
routes.basis: Grid {{cell}} m · {{w}}×{{h}} cells · current terrain (source data + approved edits).
routes.disclaimer: Planning and training tool: it supports decisions, it does not replace a safety clearance for crewed traverses.

errors.no_path: No walkable route under the current assumptions (max {{max}}°). Raise the limit or move A/B.
errors.too_far: A and B are more than 25 km apart: choose closer points.
errors.same_point: A and B are too close together.

daylight.title: Daylight budget at A
daylight.ok: Enough light: {{left}} of daylight left for a round trip of about {{walk}}.
daylight.tight: Tight: only {{left}} of daylight left for a round trip of about {{walk}}. Start earlier or shorten the walk.
daylight.night: It is night at A now. Use the time controls to plan for the next daylight window.
daylight.note: Mars24 sun position; geometric sunrise/sunset — ignores terrain shadows, refraction and twilight. Round trip = 2 × the longer route, at the Earth-heuristic pace.

routes.introRover: Today Mars is explored by robots. Compare two drives between A and B on the current terrain: the shortest and the one with gentlest slopes, using Perseverance’s published limits. Values come from elevation data; limits are assumptions you can edit.
routes.assumptionsRover: Default 24° = the tilt limit NASA’s Perseverance team set in 2026. Terrain slope on this grid is only a proxy for rover tilt: rocks under single wheels add more.
routes.driveTime: Drive time at top speed (152 m/h)
routes.roverPower: Perseverance is nuclear-powered (MMRTG), so a daylight budget does not limit it the way it limits solar rovers like Spirit and Opportunity or an astronaut on EVA. Switch to Astronaut for the daylight budget.
routes.disclaimerRover: Planning and training tool. Real drives are planned by NASA engineers with ground imagery and onboard AutoNav; MARS OS shows the terrain knowledge behind each option.

know.title: How well do we know this ground?
know.note: Rover-visited = within 50 m of Perseverance’s published traverse (NASA MMGIS). 20 m DEM = CTX stereo elevation. Coarse = MOLA only: slopes there are smoothed. Ground that no robot has crossed is the least known.
know.unvisited: {{pct}}% of the shortest route crosses ground no rover has driven. It may look gentle and still hide soft sand or rocks: this is where orbital imagery must be checked before trusting the route.

sand.title: Lesson from Spirit, built into MARS OS
sand.spirit: In 2009 Spirit drove onto ground at “Troy” (Gusev crater) that looked ordinary: a thin crust hid soft sand, and the rover stayed there for good. That is why MARS OS shows, for every route, which stretches a rover has already crossed and which are known only from orbit: planners see at a glance where to look closer.
sand.source: Spirit: NASA mission history. Open the HiRISE 25 cm layer to inspect the orbit-only stretches.

drive.title: Compare with a real Perseverance drive
drive.intro: Load the path Perseverance really drove between two sols (NASA’s published traverse). A and B are set to its start and end, and the real drive is measured with the same rules as the computed routes.
drive.none: No drive found for that sol range. Try sols where the rover moved.
drive.insight: Perseverance drove {{real}}; the shortest computed route is {{short}} ({{extra}}% difference). Steepest section on this grid: real drive {{realMax}}°, shortest {{shortMax}}°, low-slope {{lowMax}}°.
drive.why: Why they differ: rover planners also avoid hazards a slope map cannot show (sand ripples, rocks, wheel damage risk), stop at science targets, and drive where images from the ground confirm it is safe. A longer real path is not a worse one.
drive.basis: All three measured on the same grid and current terrain. No AI involved.

minerals.title: Mineral detections within 25 km
minerals.note: Orbital detections at published positions (often rounded): evidence that water-altered minerals exist nearby, not a resource estimate.

samples.nasaPhoto: NASA photo of the sampling site

highlights.1: The first coring attempt: the rock crumbled into powder, so this tube holds Martian atmosphere.
highlights.2: The first rock core sealed for possible return to Earth.
highlights.17: Regolith (loose surface material): it shows the dust and soil that future explorers and their equipment will face.
highlights.18: Regolith (loose surface material): it shows the dust and soil that future explorers and their equipment will face.
highlights.24: Carbonate cemented by silica. Carbonates form in water, so this core keeps a record of Jezero’s ancient lake.
highlights.25: Cored from the rock “Cheyava Falls”. In September 2025 NASA called its features the clearest potential biosignature found so far: not proof of life, which needs study in labs on Earth.
highlights.27: Serpentinite forms when water reacts with rock deep in the crust.

explorers.intro: NASA sends each robot to a different place, so every landing site is a piece of Mars known from the ground. Click one to see its photo, its story and how far it is from the others.
explorers.distNote: Great-circle distance over the surface between current (or final reported) positions, computed by MARS OS.
explorers.orbitersTitle: Orbiters that mapped Mars — and what MARS OS uses from them
explorers.orbitersIntro: Robots on the ground see a few kilometres; orbiters map the whole planet. These are the spacecraft behind the layers in MARS OS.

orbiters.mro: Near-polar orbit about 255–320 km up (NSSDCA). Its cameras give MARS OS the sharpest images and the 20 m terrain model of Jezero.
orbiters.odyssey: Polar orbit about 400 km up (NSSDCA). Its THEMIS camera maps day and night temperatures of the surface.
orbiters.mgs: Its laser altimeter (MOLA) measured the height of the whole planet: the base of MARS OS terrain everywhere.
orbiters.viking: The first global colour photographs of Mars, still the global base map.
orbiters.mex: ESA mission. Its OMEGA spectrometer helped map the hydrous minerals in the Resources layer.

stories.viking1: The first U.S. lander to work on Mars. It sent the first colour pictures from the surface and kept working for more than six years.
stories.viking2: Landed much farther north, in Utopia Planitia, and photographed frost on the ground during the Martian winter.
stories.pathfinder: Sojourner was the first rover on Mars: a small robot that studied the rocks around its lander in Ares Vallis.
stories.spirit: Planned for 90 sols, it explored Gusev crater for more than six years and drove 7.73 km. In 2009 its wheels broke through a crust into soft sand at “Troy”; it kept doing science as a stationary station until its last signal in March 2010. Its lesson is built into MARS OS routes.
stories.opportunity: Planned for 90 sols, it explored Meridiani Planum for almost 15 years and drove 45.16 km. A planet-wide dust storm in 2018 cut its solar power, and NASA closed the mission in February 2019.
stories.phoenix: Landed in the arctic plains and dug into the soil, confirming water ice just below the surface.
stories.curiosity: Climbing Mount Sharp in Gale crater since 2012. MARS OS loads its full drive live from NASA.
stories.insight: A stationary geophysics lander that recorded marsquakes to study the inside of the planet.
stories.perseverance: Exploring Jezero crater since 2021 and collecting rock samples. Its full drive and its 30 named samples are in MARS OS.
stories.ingenuity: The first aircraft to fly on another planet: 72 flights over Jezero, the last in January 2024. MARS OS draws its path from airfield to airfield.

explorers.stopsSource: Stops, descriptions and images: NASA Mars Trek (positions located on HiRISE images).

memories.title: {{rover}} was here · sol {{sol}} · {{d}} away
memories.note: Raw photos from the rover at this stop · NASA/JPL-Caltech · click for more
memories.trekNote: Expedition stop and image: NASA Mars Trek (HiRISE-located).

ice.title: Nearest water-ice evidence
ice.note: Icy craters: fresh impacts whose bright ice was confirmed from orbit (HiRISE, CRISM; Dundas et al. 2014) — ice within about a metre of the surface. Glacier-like forms: ice under a debris cover. Water is the first resource a crew needs: drinking, oxygen and rocket propellant. Published positions, not an ice-depth map.

landing.showOnMap: Show zones and ellipses on the map
landing.pinHint: Pin any point on the map (click the terrain) to run a landing site check, or choose an Exploration Zone below.
landing.ellipsesNote: Polygons from NASA Mars Trek. Axes and area computed by MARS OS from each polygon. Entry has uncertainties, so the spacecraft is predicted to land somewhere inside the ellipse: everything inside must be safe.
landing.zonesIntro: Candidate regions proposed at NASA’s 2015 workshop on landing sites for the first human missions. Each Exploration Zone is a {{r}} km radius area that must hold a landing site, a habitat site and regions of interest for science and resources.
landing.zonesSource: Source: NASA First Landing Site / Exploration Zone Workshop for Human Missions to the Surface of Mars (2015), via NASA Mars Trek (EZMars service, 100 km buffers).

how.title: How a landing site is chosen

elev.d: More air above low ground gives the heat shield and parachute more time to slow the spacecraft; every NASA landing site in MARS OS lies below the planet’s reference level.

lat.d: Near the equator, solar power is stronger and nights are milder; missions that look for ice, like Phoenix, go to high latitudes.

ellipse.d: The area where the spacecraft will land with high probability. It shrank from about 130 × 27 km for InSight to a few km for Perseverance, which also steered away from hazards with Terrain-Relative Navigation.

surface.d: Gentle slopes and few large rocks inside the ellipse, and ground firm enough for the lander and the rover.

science.d: The site must answer the mission’s question: Jezero for its ancient lake delta, Gale for its layered mountain.

resources.d: For humans, water ice and useful minerals within reach matter as much as safety: that is what the Exploration Zones and the ice layer show.

check.note: Measured and derived values to compare candidate sites, not a certification. Sources: MOLA elevation (NASA PDS), Mars Trek ice and mineral services, NASA MMGIS and Mars Trek positions.

welcome.title: Welcome to MARS OS
welcome.text: A living 3D atlas of Mars built on NASA data. Everything you see has a source you can open, and modelled values are labelled as such. This short tour shows the main parts; you can skip it any time.

layers.title: Map layers
layers.text: The left panel holds the maps: base imagery and elevation from orbiters, high-resolution overlays, mission data and resources. Each layer has an “i” with its source and resolution.

explorers.title: Every robot on Mars
explorers.text: The Explorers tab lists every NASA robot that reached the surface, with its photo, story, findings, instruments, expedition stops and distances between them. Curiosity’s and Perseverance’s drives load live from NASA.

resources.title: Resources for explorers
resources.text: Water ice evidence (craters that exposed ice, buried glaciers), orbital mineral detections and Perseverance’s rock samples. Pin a point and the inspector tells you how far the nearest ice is.

landing.title: Where to land
landing.text: The Landing tab explains how a site is chosen, shows real landing ellipses and the Exploration Zones NASA collected for the first human missions, and runs a factual check for any point you pin.

inspect.title: Inspect any point
inspect.text: Click the terrain to pin it: elevation with its source product, nearby minerals and ice, the editable terrain cell and the provenance of every value.

routes.title: Plan a route, watch it driven
routes.text: Compare the shortest and the gentlest route for a rover or an astronaut, load a real Perseverance drive and watch a 3D rover drive it. Each route shows its risks, how well the ground is known and a downloadable route sheet.

ai.title: AI with human approval
ai.text: Gemini analyses the evidence of a terrain cell and may propose a correction with its reasons and sources. Nothing changes the map until a person approves it.

history.title: History of the map
history.text: Every approved change is a version: compare versions, travel back in time and restore any earlier state of the terrain.

hud.title: Visor HUD
hud.text: A first-person training view in the helmet visor: compass, slope underfoot, local solar time and, near a real rover stop, the photos the rover took there. Here: Perseverance’s landing site.

mission.title: Mission Lab: your own mission
mission.text: Here a base camp sits on a crater that exposed water ice. Send a crew, a rover or a base anywhere: MARS OS calculates oxygen, energy, light time to Earth, radiation, water and EVA range, compares two sites and asks Gemini whether the mission answers its question.

rovers3d.title: Robots where they really are
rovers3d.text: Get close to the ground and each rover appears as a 3D model where it is today, or where its mission ended: Perseverance in Jezero, Curiosity in Gale, Spirit at Troy, Opportunity in Perseverance Valley.

risk.title: Route risk analysis
risk.sandInside: Sand: the route crosses mapped dune field {{id}}. Loose sand is the hazard that trapped Spirit: avoid or inspect with HiRISE.
risk.sandNear: Sand: a mapped dune field is {{d}} from the route. Check the edges for drifted sand.
risk.sandNone: Sand: no mapped dune field within {{d}} (the database maps fields, not small ripples or sand patches).
risk.slope: Slope: steepest section {{max}}°; {{share}}% of the route is steeper than the caution limit ({{c}}°).
risk.slopeOk: Slope: steepest section {{max}}°, within the caution limit.
risk.res: Data resolution: {{share}}% of the route only has coarse elevation (up to {{coarse}}/px): slopes there are smoothed.
risk.resOk: Data resolution: the whole route is on the 20 m elevation model or finer.
risk.rocks: Visible obstacles: rocks and small scarps are below the grid; HiRISE 25 cm imagery covers {{share}}% of the route.
risk.rocksHirise: Visible obstacles: HiRISE 25 cm imagery covers the route: zoom in to check rocks before relying on it.
risk.unknown: Ground knowledge: {{share}}% of the route has never been crossed by a rover.
risk.known: Ground knowledge: {{share}}% of the route is within 50 m of where a rover drove.
risk.note: Sources: Mars Global Digital Dune Database (NASA Mars Trek), the route’s elevation products, HiRISE coverage, Perseverance traverse (NASA MMGIS). Green = no issue found in these data; amber = check; red = hazard in the data.

why.title: Why does MARS OS recommend this route?
why.elev: Elevation: {{a}} ({{ra}}/px) at A and {{b}} ({{rb}}/px) at B, sampled on a {{cell}} m grid that is never finer than the data.
why.edits: Approved terrain edits in the area: {{n}} (each one is in the History tab).
why.rule: Rule: {{profile}}; impassable above {{max}}°, caution above {{caution}}°, slope weight {{w}} for the low-slope route. Fixed rules, no AI.
why.traverse: Where rovers have driven (Perseverance traverse, NASA MMGIS), to show how well each stretch is known.
why.dunes: Mapped dune fields (Mars Global Digital Dune Database) for the sand warning.
why.missing: Data MARS OS does not have here

miss.rocks: Rock abundance and obstacles smaller than the grid: only visible in HiRISE images, not used in the calculation.
miss.soil: Soil strength and thermal inertia (how soft the ground is): not used yet.
miss.fresh: Images newer than the products listed: dunes and dust can move.
miss.weather: Weather and dust storms on the day of the traverse.

why.note: The recommendation compares measured slopes only. A planner should check the missing items before using the route.

sheet.title: Route sheet
sheet.realDrive: Compared with Perseverance’s real drive, sols {{from}}–{{to}}.
sheet.edits: Approved terrain edits in the area: {{n}} ({{ids}})

rems.title: Curiosity measurements: the whole mission
rems.intro: {{n}} sols of daily summaries from Curiosity’s weather station (REMS) in Gale crater, {{from}} to {{to}}.
rems.note: The pressure rises and falls every Martian year because part of the CO2 atmosphere freezes onto the polar caps in winter and returns in spring. Daily outreach values from REMS (Centro de Astrobiología, CSIC-INTA / NASA); science data in the NASA PDS.

watch.title: New on Mars since your last visit
watch.intro: MARS OS reads NASA’s live rover feeds every time it opens.
watch.note: Gemini runs only when you ask: each analysis uses the shared quota, and any change it proposes still needs a person’s approval before it touches the map.

mission.intro: Send your own mission anywhere on Mars: a crew on EVA, a rover or a base camp. MARS OS does not stop you. It calculates what that place means for oxygen, energy, communication with Earth, radiation, water and terrain, and can ask Gemini whether the mission answers its question.
mission.noSite: No site yet: place it on the map, use the pinned point, or send an Exploration Zone from the Landing tab.
mission.questionPh: Mission question (e.g. “Can a crew reach water ice and ancient lake sediments from here?”)
mission.defaultQuestion: Can a {{kind}} work safely here and do useful exploration?
mission.assumptionsNote: Editable planning assumptions, not validated mission rules. Constants: crew O2 0.84 kg/person/day (NASA BVAD); MOXIE about 12 g O2/h (NASA); MMRTG about 110 W (NASA); surface radiation 0.64 mSv/day (MSL RAD, Hassler et al. 2014); NASA career limit 600 mSv (NASA-STD-3001).

f.pressure: Air pressure about {{p}} Pa, far below the {{a}} Pa Armstrong limit: a person needs a pressure suit at all times outside.
f.dune: The site is inside mapped dune field {{id}}: loose sand can trap wheels (Spirit, 2009) and makes footing and landing harder.
f.duneNear: A mapped dune field is {{d}} away.
f.slopeRover: Regional slope {{s}}° is above the 24° rover tilt limit.
f.slope: Regional slope {{s}}°: rough ground for walking, driving and landing.
f.sun: Average sunlight at the surface is only about {{w}} W/m²: solar power is weak here (latitude, season or dust).
f.conj: Solar conjunction during the mission: about {{n}} days without reliable contact with Earth, starting on day {{first}}.
f.rad: Surface radiation alone uses {{p}}% of NASA’s career limit.
f.iceInRange: A crater that exposed water ice is within the EVA range.
f.iceFar: Nearest water-ice evidence is {{d}} away: water must be carried, mined from minerals or reached by vehicle.
f.polar: High latitude: long polar nights and very cold winters.

o2.title: Oxygen
o2.note: 0.84 kg O2 per person per day (NASA BVAD). MOXIE made oxygen from the Martian air at up to about 12 g per hour (NASA); a crew would need much larger systems: this shows the scale.

energy.title: Energy
energy.rtg: MMRTG-sized generators for the same power
energy.roverSolar: Solar rover energy per sol ({{m2}} m² panels)
energy.note: Computed from latitude, season and Sun distance (Mars24) with a rough dust attenuation e^−τ that ignores diffuse light. Dust storms can push τ above 4 (this is how Opportunity lost power in 2018).

comms.title: Communication with Earth
comms.conj: Solar conjunction in the mission window
comms.note: Computed from JPL approximate orbital elements at the date in the clock. Near solar conjunction (Sun within about 3° of Mars) missions pause commanding; relay orbiters carry most of the data.

rad.title: Radiation
rad.note: Measured rate 0.64 ± 0.12 mSv/day at Gale (MSL RAD, Hassler et al. 2014). The trip to Mars adds about 1.8 mSv per day of cruise (MSL RAD, Zeitlin et al. 2013). Shielding with regolith lowers the surface dose.

eva.title: EVA range from here
eva.stops: Robot expedition stops within the radius
eva.note: Radius = walking speed × EVA time × (1 − reserve) ÷ 2, on flat ground. Slopes, rocks and suit limits reduce it; the green ring on the map shows it.

ai.title: Does this mission answer its question?
ai.note: Gemini only saw the facts and assumptions above. Planning aid, not a safety certification.

mission.compareNote: Bold = the better value for each row by a simple rule (lower, gentler, closer to ice, more minerals, more sunlight). Which site is “best” depends on the mission question.
mission.sources: Sources: MOLA elevation (NASA PDS), Mars Trek ice, mineral and dune services, NASA Mars Trek and MMGIS positions, Mars24 sun geometry, JPL orbital elements, NASA BVAD, MSL RAD, NASA-STD-3001.
